chapters.title: 1. Introduction
chapters.summary: The argument: effect handlers subsume control features (exceptions, iterators, backtracking, async) that languages usually build in, so async can be a library.

chapters.title: 2. Overview
chapters.summary: A quick course in Koka handlers: declaring effects and operations, handlers that resume or abort, state as a handler, iterators, and handlers that resume more than once.

chapters.title: 3. Asynchronous Programming
chapters.summary: Async as an effect: an await operation handled on the event loop, then structured features built on it: interleaving with safely encapsulated state, cancellation and resource release, promises, and ambient state.

chapters.title: 4. Semantics
chapters.summary: A typed core calculus for handlers: syntax, row-typed effects (as in the Koka MSFP paper), typing rules, an operational semantics, and how handlers relate to delimited continuations (shift/reset).

title: Structured Asynchrony with Algebraic Effects
byline: Daan Leijen · Microsoft Research technical report MSR-TR-2017-21 (2017)
note: PDF pages match the report’s pages (1–14). The conclusion and references are not broken out. This is not the POPL 2017 *Type Directed Compilation of Row-Typed Algebraic Effects* paper, which is still missing from Drive. Summaries are in our own words; the text stays in the PDF.
summary: Shows that async/await needs no compiler support once a language has algebraic effect handlers. After a tour of handlers in Koka (exceptions, resumable operations, state, iterators, multiple resumptions), the report builds an async effect whose handler sits on the Node.js event loop, then adds block-scoped interleaving, cancellation with resource release, timeouts, promises and ambient state that is local to one strand of asynchronous execution. It closes with a small typed calculus and operational semantics for handlers and compares them with delimited continuations. Close in spirit to how Kyo implements Async, Abort and resource safety as handled effects.
